foundations.title: Professional Foundations — Northern Ireland
foundations.action: Explain the purpose of contact, professional role and confidentiality limits in accessible language.
foundations.record: Identify the HSC Trust, provider and any statutory appointment relevant to the task. Use supervision to test how poverty, disability, trauma or barriers to services influence the formulation. Link learning and feedback to the current NISCC registration and professional-development requirements. Explain the relevant Trust or provider complaint route and when a concern about a registered worker belongs with NISCC. Give the person a clear account of who can address the outcome they seek; professional regulation does not itself arrange a care package.

care-support.title: Social Care and Support — Northern Ireland
care-support.action: Describe the person’s needs and desired outcomes, including fluctuation and the effect of unavailable support.
care-support.record: Ask the Trust to explain the assessment and eligibility decisions separately from costs and provision. Offer a carer’s assessment where the relevant conditions are met, including consideration of young carers. Compare arranged services with direct payments and confirm that the proposed support can actually be delivered. Request reasons, reassessment where circumstances change and the appropriate Trust complaint or review route. Record interim arrangements and unmet needs while a decision is disputed. NI Direct explains access, carers’ assessments and direct payments, with links to local services.

mca.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — Northern Ireland
mca.action: Identify the proposed act and confirm that the provision being relied on is commenced for that purpose.
mca.record: Specify the decision and provide practical support before applying the relevant capacity test. Check whether the required assessment must be completed by a suitably qualified and trained person. Record the person’s wishes, consultation and the actual legal basis for any decision taken without their own consent. For phase-1 deprivation-of-liberty decisions, check the Review Tribunal route and safeguards in the current Code, forms and interim guidance. For another type of decision, obtain advice about the applicable law rather than extending phase-1 powers by analogy.

dols.title: Restrictions and Liberty — Northern Ireland
dols.action: Describe actual arrangements and obtain evidence about the person’s wishes, understanding and objections.
dols.record: Consult the current interim guidance before deciding whether the arrangements amount to deprivation of liberty. Use the appropriate trained assessors, Trust process and current forms where an authorisation is required. Keep capacity, best interests, authorisation, consultation and challenge arrangements separately recorded. Identify the nominated person, advocacy or representation required and the person’s access to the Review Tribunal. Check expiry, review and changed circumstances. Do not remove an existing safeguard solely because a judgment or guidance has changed without the responsible legal review.

mha.title: Mental Health — Northern Ireland
mha.action: Identify voluntary support and whether an assessment or treatment detention route is actually being considered.
mha.record: Check the current Order, evidence for the particular criteria and the authorised professional’s role. Keep the partly commenced capacity framework and any separate physical-treatment decision distinct. Explain the person’s status and arrange rights information, support and review under the applicable route. The Review Tribunal and the relevant hospital discharge or review processes address detention questions. Help the person obtain advice and understand how to challenge the measure. Confirm which rules apply to their specific admission status and documents.

safeguarding.title: Adult Safeguarding — Northern Ireland
safeguarding.action: Identify abuse, exploitation or neglect and the adult’s ability to protect themselves in their actual circumstances.
safeguarding.record: Use the organisation’s safeguarding arrangements and refer protection concerns to the appropriate HSC Trust route. Contact PSNI where the circumstances require a police response, distinguishing criminal investigation from the support plan. Establish the lawful basis for information sharing and for any proposed intervention without agreement. Use the policy’s participation and proportionate-response approach, together with the applicable consent, capacity and legal safeguards. Explain the Trust or provider complaint process and obtain specialist advice if a coercive intervention is proposed.

children.title: Children, Families and Transitions — Northern Ireland
children.action: Record the child’s account, daily experience, harm concerns and support needs.
children.record: Use the current regional policy and Trust referral procedure for a child-protection concern. Identify who holds parental responsibility and any court order affecting the proposed decision. Coordinate education, health and family support and plan transitions before a service ends. Explain the particular assessment, protection or court process, including how the child and family can participate, obtain advocacy or legal advice and raise disagreement. Do not promise confidentiality that conflicts with a necessary safeguarding response.

rights.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — Northern Ireland
rights.action: Identify the relevant equality law and public-authority duty for the actual decision.
rights.record: Arrange accessible communication and consider the applicable reasonable-adjustment obligations. Establish the purpose and legal basis of sharing, including the treatment of sensitive information. Record the person’s account, alternatives, reasons, disagreement and the route for correction or challenge. The Equality Commission for Northern Ireland provides information on discrimination and routes to challenge. Distinguish a service complaint, an equality-scheme concern and legal proceedings; obtain timely advice because different limits and remedies apply.

sources.title: Northern Ireland Source Library
sources.action: Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.
sources.record: Record the exact source and provision used, date accessed and any unresolved question.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Northern Ireland practice guide?
cards.answer: The Northern Ireland Social Care Council (NISCC) Standards of Conduct and Practice provide the professional framework for registered social workers. Distinguish those standards from the procedures of a Health and Social Care (HSC) Trust and from powers available only to a specifically trained or appointed practitioner.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: HSC Trusts provide important health and social-care functions; the Regulation and Quality Improvement Authority (RQIA) has a separate service-regulation role. Identify the actual decision-maker and employer. A concern about a worker’s professional conduct, a provider’s quality and a Trust’s care decision may need different responses.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Explain the purpose of contact, professional role and confidentiality limits in accessible language. Identify the HSC Trust, provider and any statutory appointment relevant to the task. Use supervision to test how poverty, disability, trauma or barriers to services influence the formulation. Link learning and feedback to the current NISCC registration and professional-development requirements.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Explain the relevant Trust or provider complaint route and when a concern about a registered worker belongs with NISCC. Give the person a clear account of who can address the outcome they seek; professional regulation does not itself arrange a care package.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating “the Trust decided” as sufficient explanation without identifying the decision, authority and reasons.

flashcardDecks.title: Social Care and Support — Northern Ireland

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Northern Ireland practice guide?
cards.answer: An HSC Trust needs assessment is the starting point for community support. The Health and Personal Social Services (Northern Ireland) Order 1972 and the Carers and Direct Payments Act (Northern Ireland) 2002 form part of the legal map. Establish the particular duty, Trust criteria and service being requested.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Direct payments can allow an eligible person to arrange assessed support. Discuss the option during assessment, including consent, the ability to manage it with support, permitted use and employer responsibilities. A carer’s own assessment concerns their caring role and needs; it does not replace the assessment of the person receiving care.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Describe the person’s needs and desired outcomes, including fluctuation and the effect of unavailable support. Ask the Trust to explain the assessment and eligibility decisions separately from costs and provision. Offer a carer’s assessment where the relevant conditions are met, including consideration of young carers. Compare arranged services with direct payments and confirm that the proposed support can actually be delivered.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Request reasons, reassessment where circumstances change and the appropriate Trust complaint or review route. Record interim arrangements and unmet needs while a decision is disputed. NI Direct explains access, carers’ assessments and direct payments, with links to local services.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Confusing the carer’s support with services for the cared-for person, or describing an unpaid family arrangement as an agreed funded plan.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Northern Ireland practice guide?
cards.answer: The Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 is only partly commenced. Phase 1 covers research and specified deprivation-of-liberty and money-and-valuables provisions. Do not apply the whole Act as though it were already the general framework for every treatment or welfare decision.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Within the operative framework, the assessment is decision-specific, with support before a conclusion of incapacity. The inability must result from impairment or disturbance of the mind or brain. Test understanding, retaining information for the decision, appreciating its relevance and using and weighing it, and communicating the choice. Record how any failed ability affects this decision, rather than relying on a diagnosis. The principles address capacity and best interests. Formal assessments and other statutory functions have training and qualification requirements. A nominated person must be consulted in the relevant process; the role does not confer general substitute decision-making authority.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the proposed act and confirm that the provision being relied on is commenced for that purpose. Specify the decision and provide practical support before applying the relevant capacity test. Check whether the required assessment must be completed by a suitably qualified and trained person. Record the person’s wishes, consultation and the actual legal basis for any decision taken without their own consent.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: For phase-1 deprivation-of-liberty decisions, check the Review Tribunal route and safeguards in the current Code, forms and interim guidance. For another type of decision, obtain advice about the applicable law rather than extending phase-1 powers by analogy.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Assuming full commencement or treating the nominated person as a universal decision-maker.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Northern Ireland practice guide?
cards.answer: The operative deprivation-of-liberty provisions of the Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 require the relevant assessments, authorisation and safeguards. Setting, age, purpose and the applicable mental-health or children’s framework must be established before selecting a route.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The Department of Health states that the Supreme Court judgment of 2 June 2026 changed the previous approach to defining deprivation of liberty. Interim guidance is available while the Code and other material are reviewed. Read that guidance with current Trust specialist advice; an older training slide is not sufficient evidence of the current legal test.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Describe actual arrangements and obtain evidence about the person’s wishes, understanding and objections. Consult the current interim guidance before deciding whether the arrangements amount to deprivation of liberty. Use the appropriate trained assessors, Trust process and current forms where an authorisation is required. Keep capacity, best interests, authorisation, consultation and challenge arrangements separately recorded.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Identify the nominated person, advocacy or representation required and the person’s access to the Review Tribunal. Check expiry, review and changed circumstances. Do not remove an existing safeguard solely because a judgment or guidance has changed without the responsible legal review.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating an old definition, a completed form or family approval as a complete legal analysis.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Northern Ireland practice guide?
cards.answer: The Mental Health (Northern Ireland) Order 1986 remains relevant alongside the partly commenced capacity legislation. Assessment and treatment routes have their own criteria and professional roles. For admission for assessment, the Order includes mental disorder of a nature or degree warranting detention for assessment and the relevant substantial likelihood of serious physical harm.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: An approved social worker has specific training and functions. The medical recommendation, application and hospital processes should be distinguished. A general referral to mental-health services is not a compulsory admission application.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify voluntary support and whether an assessment or treatment detention route is actually being considered. Check the current Order, evidence for the particular criteria and the authorised professional’s role. Keep the partly commenced capacity framework and any separate physical-treatment decision distinct. Explain the person’s status and arrange rights information, support and review under the applicable route.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The Review Tribunal and the relevant hospital discharge or review processes address detention questions. Help the person obtain advice and understand how to challenge the measure. Confirm which rules apply to their specific admission status and documents.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Assuming the 2016 capacity legislation has replaced every mental-health admission provision.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Northern Ireland practice guide?
cards.answer: The regional policy Adult Safeguarding: Prevention and Protection in Partnership distinguishes an adult at risk of harm from an adult in need of protection. It considers personal characteristics and life circumstances, with HSC Trust and PSNI roles according to the concern. It is not a general power to compel an adult to accept services.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The Adult Protection Bill is a reform to monitor, not a source of powers to assume are already operational. The Assembly’s legislative tracker must be checked for passage and any subsequent Act and commencement before applying a new duty.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify abuse, exploitation or neglect and the adult’s ability to protect themselves in their actual circumstances. Use the organisation’s safeguarding arrangements and refer protection concerns to the appropriate HSC Trust route. Contact PSNI where the circumstances require a police response, distinguishing criminal investigation from the support plan. Establish the lawful basis for information sharing and for any proposed intervention without agreement.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Use the policy’s participation and proportionate-response approach, together with the applicable consent, capacity and legal safeguards. Explain the Trust or provider complaint process and obtain specialist advice if a coercive intervention is proposed.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating a safeguarding policy as a detention power or treating a proposed Bill as commenced law.

flashcardDecks.title: Children, Families and Transitions — Northern Ireland

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Northern Ireland practice guide?
cards.answer: The Children (Northern Ireland) Order 1995 provides the main framework for children in need, family support and protective court processes. Co-operating to Safeguard Children and Young People supplies the regional policy framework. The HSC Trust’s children’s services and PSNI have different responsibilities.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Assessment and family support should be distinguished from a protection investigation or court order. A family meeting cannot create powers of removal or determine legal parental responsibility. Check the child’s position and the relevant authority for accommodation, contact and treatment decisions.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Record the child’s account, daily experience, harm concerns and support needs. Use the current regional policy and Trust referral procedure for a child-protection concern. Identify who holds parental responsibility and any court order affecting the proposed decision. Coordinate education, health and family support and plan transitions before a service ends.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Explain the particular assessment, protection or court process, including how the child and family can participate, obtain advocacy or legal advice and raise disagreement. Do not promise confidentiality that conflicts with a necessary safeguarding response.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Allowing an internal discussion or a parent’s request for secrecy to replace the required protection response.

flashcardDecks.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — Northern Ireland

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Northern Ireland practice guide?
cards.answer: Northern Ireland has its own equality laws. The Equality Act 2010 does not apply. Identify the relevant disability, sex, race, religious or political discrimination provision and the setting it covers. Section 75 of the Northern Ireland Act 1998 places equality-of-opportunity and good-relations duties on designated public authorities.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The Human Rights Act and applicable UK data-protection law also matter, but they answer different questions. A public authority’s equality scheme does not by itself establish permission to disclose a person’s health information.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the relevant equality law and public-authority duty for the actual decision. Arrange accessible communication and consider the applicable reasonable-adjustment obligations. Establish the purpose and legal basis of sharing, including the treatment of sensitive information. Record the person’s account, alternatives, reasons, disagreement and the route for correction or challenge.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The Equality Commission for Northern Ireland provides information on discrimination and routes to challenge. Distinguish a service complaint, an equality-scheme concern and legal proceedings; obtain timely advice because different limits and remedies apply.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Copying an equality test from another legal system or equating identical treatment with accessible participation.

glossaryTerms.definition: The Northern Ireland Social Care Council (NISCC) Standards of Conduct and Practice provide the professional framework for registered social workers. Distinguish those standards from the procedures of a Health and Social Care (HSC) Trust and from powers available only to a specifically trained or appointed practitioner.

An HSC Trust needs assessment is the starting point for community support. The Health and Personal Social Services (Northern Ireland) Order 1972 and the Carers and Direct Payments Act (Northern Ireland) 2002 form part of the legal map. Establish the particular duty, Trust criteria and service being requested.

The Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 is only partly commenced. Phase 1 covers research and specified deprivation-of-liberty and money-and-valuables provisions. Do not apply the whole Act as though it were already the general framework for every treatment or welfare decision.

The operative deprivation-of-liberty provisions of the Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 require the relevant assessments, authorisation and safeguards. Setting, age, purpose and the applicable mental-health or children’s framework must be established before selecting a route.

The Mental Health (Northern Ireland) Order 1986 remains relevant alongside the partly commenced capacity legislation. Assessment and treatment routes have their own criteria and professional roles. For admission for assessment, the Order includes mental disorder of a nature or degree warranting detention for assessment and the relevant substantial likelihood of serious physical harm.

The regional policy Adult Safeguarding: Prevention and Protection in Partnership distinguishes an adult at risk of harm from an adult in need of protection. It considers personal characteristics and life circumstances, with HSC Trust and PSNI roles according to the concern. It is not a general power to compel an adult to accept services.

The Children (Northern Ireland) Order 1995 provides the main framework for children in need, family support and protective court processes. Co-operating to Safeguard Children and Young People supplies the regional policy framework. The HSC Trust’s children’s services and PSNI have different responsibilities.

Northern Ireland has its own equality laws. The Equality Act 2010 does not apply. Identify the relevant disability, sex, race, religious or political discrimination provision and the setting it covers. Section 75 of the Northern Ireland Act 1998 places equality-of-opportunity and good-relations duties on designated public authorities.
The professional body identified for this guide. Check its remit and the requirements that apply to your role.
Support to express views, understand choices and participate; statutory entitlements depend on the local framework.
Continuing professional development: learning, reflection and evidence of improvement.
Agreement to a specific action; check the applicable requirements for information, voluntariness and ability to consent.
Pressure or control that can affect expressed wishes and freedom to act.
The criteria for a particular service or programme; distinct from a description of need.
Ability to make the relevant decision under the applicable legal framework; avoid a global label.
Someone with a defined support or decision-making role; verify the source and scope of authority.
A reasoned comparison of intended benefit, burdens, rights and alternatives.
Attention to power, identity and the person’s experience of a service, informed by their preferences.
Using or sharing only information needed for an identified lawful purpose.
Protecting information while understanding and explaining lawful exceptions.
Communicating a concern to the appropriate agency; confirm the applicable route and follow-up.
Structured discussion of decisions, ethics, skills, wellbeing and accountability.
A reasoned account connecting evidence and possible explanations to a plan.
Relationships that may offer support; availability, safety and willingness need assessment.
Planned change between services or life stages, with continuity and named responsibilities.
An agreed response if risks increase or the preferred plan cannot operate.
A planned check of outcomes, changing circumstances and whether actions remain appropriate.
An option that can achieve the purpose with less interference in rights and freedom.

theoryLenses.title: Ecological Systems Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Person, family, housing, community, services, poverty, policy, culture, and environment.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be shaped by pressures around the person, not only by individual behaviour or choice.
test: What changed in the environment before the concern escalated?
Which systems are supporting the person, and which are adding pressure?
Would risk reduce if housing, income, access, care, or community support changed?

theoryLenses.title: Strengths-Based Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Capabilities, identity, relationships, community, culture, hope, and what is already working.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may have protective strategies or relationships that are hidden by a risk-heavy professional account.
test: What has helped the person survive or cope so far?
Who does the person trust, and what role could they safely play?
Which strengths are real evidence, and which are optimistic assumptions?

theoryLenses.title: Trauma-Informed Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment, shame, threat responses, and control.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Behaviour that looks like refusal, avoidance, anger, or disengagement may be a survival response to trauma, coercion, loss, or fear.
test: What might feel unsafe or controlling from the person's perspective?
What helps the person feel more choice and predictability?
How can we avoid repeating patterns of powerlessness?

theoryLenses.title: Attachment Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Trust, separation, dependency, rejection, fear, care-seeking, and relationship patterns.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Responses to professionals or carers may reflect previous experiences of care, loss, abandonment, or unsafe relationships.
test: How does the person respond when support increases, reduces, or changes?
Are there patterns of clinging, pushing away, testing, mistrust, or fear?
What relationship approach is consistent, boundaried, and safe?

theoryLenses.title: Systems and Family Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Roles, rules, communication, repeated patterns, conflict, care dynamics, and network effects.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The concern may be maintained by relationship patterns, family roles, service responses, or network conflict.
test: Who gains or loses if the current pattern changes?
What role has each person been placed in or taken on?
How do professional responses affect the family or network pattern?

theoryLenses.title: Anti-Oppressive and Anti-Discriminatory Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Power, oppression, racism, disability, class, gender, sexuality, culture, age, stigma, and access.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be intensified by structural inequality, professional power, discrimination, or inaccessible services.
test: What barriers has the person faced before we became involved?
Whose account is being treated as most credible, and why?
What reasonable adjustments, cultural humility, or advocacy are needed?

theoryLenses.title: Crisis Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Immediate stress, narrowed options, temporary disequilibrium, coping capacity, and stabilisation.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person or family may be temporarily overwhelmed and need stabilisation before longer-term planning is realistic.
test: What immediate event or loss has exceeded usual coping?
What needs to happen in the next 24 to 72 hours?
What can wait until safety, sleep, food, medication, or support is more stable?

theoryLenses.title: Life Course Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Transitions, cumulative disadvantage, ageing, identity, loss, timing, and turning points.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Current risk or distress may connect to earlier life events, cumulative exclusion, transition, bereavement, or changing identity.
test: What transitions or losses are happening now?
How has cumulative disadvantage shaped options and trust?
What strengths, relationships, or identities from earlier life still matter?

theoryLenses.title: Task-Centred Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Specific problems, agreed goals, small steps, roles, review, and measurable change.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may benefit from breaking an overwhelming issue into concrete, negotiated tasks with clear review.
test: What problem does the person most want to work on first?
What is the smallest useful next step?
Who will do what, by when, and how will we know it helped?

hypothesisSignals.label: Self-neglect, hoarding, home conditions, or repeated crisis presentations.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Think about trauma, executive functioning, environment, identity, isolation, loss, and safeguarding thresholds.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person appears to refuse support, miss visits, or disengage.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Avoid jumping straight to non-compliance. Consider trust, trauma, power, communication, and whether the offer fits the person.

hypothesisSignals.label: Family conflict, carer strain, coercion, or unclear roles are present.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Map roles, power, risk, protective factors, and what happens when professionals intervene.

hypothesisSignals.label: Risk has escalated quickly or a crisis is dominating the assessment.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Separate immediate stabilisation from longer-term formulation and legal route decisions.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is a transition: adolescence to adulthood, hospital discharge, bereavement, moving home, or ageing.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Transitions can disrupt identity, support, eligibility, relationships, and coping.

hypothesisSignals.label: Discrimination, poverty, inaccessible services, stigma, or cultural misunderstanding may be relevant.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Test whether systems are creating or worsening the difficulty.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person or carer feels overwhelmed and cannot see a way forward.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Consider crisis, small steps, stabilisation, advocacy, and practical environmental change.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is mistrust of professionals, fear of services, or repeated complaints.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Explore previous experiences, power, communication, consistency, and whether the person has reason to feel unsafe.

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Safety
childPracticeModels.use: Child protection mapping, danger statements, safety goals, family network work, scaling, and safety planning.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What are we worried about, what is working well, and what needs to happen for the child to be safe enough?
test: Can worries be written in plain language that the family understands?
What existing safety has been demonstrated, not just promised?
Who is in the family network and what role can they safely take?

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Wellbeing, Success, and Belonging
childPracticeModels.use: Family support, children in care, permanency, reunification, stability, identity, and belonging work.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What would wellbeing, safety, permanence, connection, and belonging look like from the child's perspective?
test: What does the child say or show about where they feel safe and connected?
What would meaningful stability look like in daily life?
How are family relationships, identity, culture, and belonging being protected?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Whole-family child protection where parental domestic abuse, mental health, substance misuse, trauma, or adult needs affect child safety.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety may improve when adult needs and risks are addressed alongside direct work with the child and family network.
test: Which adult needs are directly affecting child safety or care?
Is the plan joined up across children's and adults' services?
Are adult-focused interventions linked to measurable child safety outcomes?

childPracticeModels.title: Contextual Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Extra-familial harm, exploitation, peer group risk, school, neighbourhood, online spaces, and adolescent safeguarding.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Harm may be located outside the home, in peer, school, community, or online contexts that parents cannot control alone.
test: Where is harm happening: home, school, peer group, community, online, or transport?
Which context needs intervention, not only which child or parent?
Who has power or influence in that context?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Group Conferencing
childPracticeModels.use: Family-led planning, kinship care, safety planning, pre-proceedings, reunification, and support network building.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The wider family network may hold safe, practical solutions that have not yet been fully mapped or invited in.
test: Who does the child identify as family or trusted network?
What information does the family need before private planning?
How will the plan be checked for safety, clarity, and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Systemic Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Family patterns, repeated cycles, communication, roles, meaning, conflict, and relationship-based formulation.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The concern may be maintained by family patterns, relationship roles, service responses, or repeated cycles.
test: What pattern repeats, and what keeps it going?
How does each person make sense of the problem?
What would change if one part of the system responded differently?

childPracticeModels.title: Motivational Interviewing
childPracticeModels.use: Ambivalence, parental engagement, adolescent risk, substance use, resistance, and behaviour change conversations.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The parent or young person may be caught between reasons to change and reasons to keep things as they are.
test: What does the person want to be different?
What are their reasons for change and reasons against change?
Are we arguing for change so hard that the person argues against it?

childPracticeModels.title: Solution-Focused Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Goal-setting, exceptions, scaling, strengths, future-focused planning, and building on small signs of progress.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Small exceptions or signs of safety may reveal what can be repeated, strengthened, and built into the plan.
test: When is the problem slightly less serious?
What would one point higher on the safety scale look like?
What has the family already done that helped, even briefly?

childPracticeModels.title: PACE and DDP-Informed Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Children affected by trauma, attachment disruption, care experience, shame, mistrust, and blocked trust.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The child may need relational safety through playfulness, acceptance, curiosity, and empathy before they can reflect or change.
test: How does the child's behaviour make sense as communication or protection?
How can adults stay curious without shaming or escalating?
What helps the child experience safety in the relationship?

childPracticeModels.title: Safe and Together
childPracticeModels.use: Domestic abuse-informed child welfare, perpetrator pattern mapping, protective parent strengths, and child impact.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety work should focus on the perpetrator's pattern of behaviour and avoid blaming the non-abusive parent for the abuse.
test: What is the perpetrator's pattern and impact on the child?
What has the protective parent done to promote safety?
Does the plan increase accountability for the person causing harm?

childPracticeModels.title: Graded Care Profile 2
childPracticeModels.use: Neglect assessment, evidence-based care mapping, physical care, safety, love and esteem, and developmental care.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The quality of care may need structured, observable mapping rather than vague descriptions of neglect.
test: Which care domains are strong, inconsistent, or harmful?
What evidence has been observed rather than assumed?
Is change measurable across time and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Restorative Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Repair, accountability, family meetings, school relationships, conflict, shame, and shared problem-solving.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Progress may come through relationship repair, accountability, and shared planning rather than only professional direction.
test: Who has been affected and what do they need?
What repair or accountability is realistic and safe?
How will the meeting avoid blame and keep the child central?

childModelSignals.label: Child protection concerns, safety planning, or danger statements are needed.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs clear worries, existing safety, safety goals, family network planning, and review.

childModelSignals.label: Neglect, home conditions, missed health needs, or inconsistent care are central.
childModelSignals.detail: The assessment needs observable evidence, care domains, impact on the child, and change over time.

childModelSignals.label: Domestic abuse is affecting the child or family safety.
childModelSignals.detail: The plan needs perpetrator pattern analysis, protective parent strengths, child impact, and safe information sharing.

childModelSignals.label: Exploitation, adolescent risk, peer harm, school risk, or online/community harm is present.
childModelSignals.detail: Risk may sit outside the home and require contextual mapping beyond parent-focused plans.

childModelSignals.label: The child is in care, on the edge of care, returning home, or permanence is uncertain.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs belonging, stability, identity, relationships, family network options, and safe permanence planning.

childModelSignals.label: Trauma, attachment disruption, mistrust, shame, or relational conflict is central.
childModelSignals.detail: The child may need relational safety and adults who can stay curious, calm, boundaried, and empathic.

childModelSignals.label: There may be wider family or trusted network members who could help.
childModelSignals.detail: The network may hold safe options for care, practical support, supervision, or belonging.

childModelSignals.label: A parent or young person feels ambivalent, defensive, stuck, or hard to engage.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs careful engagement, change talk, respect for autonomy, and clarity about non-negotiable safety.

childModelSignals.label: There has been conflict, harm, school exclusion, relationship breakdown, or a need for repair.
childModelSignals.detail: The work may need accountability, safe dialogue, relationship repair, and a shared plan.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Professional Foundations — Northern Ireland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A family receives different explanations from a Trust worker and a commissioned provider about why visits have reduced.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Establish who changed the assessed plan and who changed delivery. Obtain the recorded decision and reasons, hear the person’s experience and address immediate unmet needs. Escalate the appropriate assessment or contract issue instead of referring every complaint to the professional regulator.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Social Care and Support — Northern Ireland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A disabled parent needs morning assistance. Their teenager is missing school to help, and a relative suggests using the parent’s benefits to pay informally.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Assess the parent’s support needs and the impact on the young person. Consider Trust-arranged care or an eligible direct-payment arrangement with proper support. Clarify funding and employment responsibilities; do not assume the child can continue filling a gap in services.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — Northern Ireland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A hospital team asks a nominated person to sign consent for an unrelated operation because a deprivation-of-liberty assessment has been completed.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Separate the operation from the liberty arrangements. Check the patient’s ability to decide about that treatment and the applicable consent law. The nominated-person role and a liberty assessment do not provide a general consent signature for another intervention.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Restrictions and Liberty — Northern Ireland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A care setting continues to use an old checklist after June 2026 and says its completed form proves all arrangements are lawful.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Review the actual restrictions and the source version used. Ask the Trust’s MCA team to apply the current guidance and determine any required reassessment or authorisation. Continue meeting immediate care and participation duties while resolving the legal position.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Mental Health — Northern Ireland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A person declines admission after an argument at home but agrees to a same-day assessment and support from a trusted friend.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Explore the immediate safety evidence, physical health and whether voluntary arrangements are workable. Ask the authorised professionals to assess the actual statutory criteria if compulsion is proposed. Refusal of the first offer is not itself the required harm analysis.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Adult Safeguarding — Northern Ireland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: An isolated adult says a neighbour takes their pension but fears losing the only person who buys groceries.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Arrange a safe conversation and practical alternatives for food and contact. Assess the protection concern and report through the relevant Trust and police routes as appropriate. A refusal of one intervention does not remove the need to explore coercion, dependency and a safer support plan.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Children, Families and Transitions — Northern Ireland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A child tells a school worker they are frightened to return home. The parent asks for the conversation to remain within school.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Listen without leading questions, record the child’s words and assess immediate safety. Follow the relevant Trust and police referral arrangements where required. Explain confidentiality limits safely and establish who will act before the child leaves the setting.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — Northern Ireland
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A service offers an assessment in an inaccessible building and says its policy treats every applicant identically.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Identify the disability-related barrier and the applicable adjustment duty. Offer an accessible arrangement and revisit any adverse inference caused by the failed appointment. Record the change and how the person can challenge the earlier decision.

printableTemplates.title: Professional Foundations
printableTemplates.summary: Explain your professional role, distinguish an ethical concern from a statutory power, and turn a formulation into an accountable plan.
printableTemplates.body:
Professional Foundations
Northern Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Northern Ireland Social Care Council (NISCC) Standards of Conduct and Practice provide the professional framework for registered social workers. Distinguish those standards from the procedures of a Health and Social Care (HSC) Trust and from powers available only to a specifically trained or appointed practitioner.

HSC Trusts provide important health and social-care functions; the Regulation and Quality Improvement Authority (RQIA) has a separate service-regulation role. Identify the actual decision-maker and employer. A concern about a worker’s professional conduct, a provider’s quality and a Trust’s care decision may need different responses.

Local pathway:
Explain the purpose of contact, professional role and confidentiality limits in accessible language.
Identify the HSC Trust, provider and any statutory appointment relevant to the task.
Use supervision to test how poverty, disability, trauma or barriers to services influence the formulation.
Link learning and feedback to the current NISCC registration and professional-development requirements.

Recording prompts:
1. Your role and the legal or professional framework
Notes:

2. The person’s outcomes and communication preferences
Notes:

3. Evidence, competing explanations and missing perspectives
Notes:

4. Power, boundaries and any conflict of interest
Notes:

5. Agreed action, supervision, feedback and review
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain the relevant Trust or provider complaint route and when a concern about a registered worker belongs with NISCC. Give the person a clear account of who can address the outcome they seek; professional regulation does not itself arrange a care package.

Sources:
https://niscc.info/standards-and-guidance/

printableTemplates.title: Social Care and Support
printableTemplates.summary: Map assessment, eligibility, funding and delivery separately; include family support without assuming it; explain the local route for challenging a decision.
printableTemplates.body:
Social Care and Support
Northern Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
An HSC Trust needs assessment is the starting point for community support. The Health and Personal Social Services (Northern Ireland) Order 1972 and the Carers and Direct Payments Act (Northern Ireland) 2002 form part of the legal map. Establish the particular duty, Trust criteria and service being requested.

Direct payments can allow an eligible person to arrange assessed support. Discuss the option during assessment, including consent, the ability to manage it with support, permitted use and employer responsibilities. A carer’s own assessment concerns their caring role and needs; it does not replace the assessment of the person receiving care.

Local pathway:
Describe the person’s needs and desired outcomes, including fluctuation and the effect of unavailable support.
Ask the Trust to explain the assessment and eligibility decisions separately from costs and provision.
Offer a carer’s assessment where the relevant conditions are met, including consideration of young carers.
Compare arranged services with direct payments and confirm that the proposed support can actually be delivered.

Recording prompts:
1. Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
Notes:

2. The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
Notes:

3. Carer willingness and separately identified needs
Notes:

4. Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
Notes:

5. Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Request reasons, reassessment where circumstances change and the appropriate Trust complaint or review route. Record interim arrangements and unmet needs while a decision is disputed. NI Direct explains access, carers’ assessments and direct payments, with links to local services.

Sources:
https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/arranging-health-and-social-care
https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/direct-payments-care
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nia/2002/6/contents

printableTemplates.title: Decision-Making and Capacity
printableTemplates.summary: Identify the precise decision, provide practical decision support, apply the local capacity or consent framework and verify a representative’s authority.
printableTemplates.body:
Decision-Making and Capacity
Northern Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 is only partly commenced. Phase 1 covers research and specified deprivation-of-liberty and money-and-valuables provisions. Do not apply the whole Act as though it were already the general framework for every treatment or welfare decision.

Within the operative framework, the assessment is decision-specific, with support before a conclusion of incapacity. The inability must result from impairment or disturbance of the mind or brain. Test understanding, retaining information for the decision, appreciating its relevance and using and weighing it, and communicating the choice. Record how any failed ability affects this decision, rather than relying on a diagnosis. The principles address capacity and best interests. Formal assessments and other statutory functions have training and qualification requirements. A nominated person must be consulted in the relevant process; the role does not confer general substitute decision-making authority.

Local pathway:
Identify the proposed act and confirm that the provision being relied on is commenced for that purpose.
Specify the decision and provide practical support before applying the relevant capacity test.
Check whether the required assessment must be completed by a suitably qualified and trained person.
Record the person’s wishes, consultation and the actual legal basis for any decision taken without their own consent.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, options and time at which it is needed
Notes:

2. Communication support and observed responses
Notes:

3. Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
Notes:

4. Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
Notes:

5. Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action
Notes:

Challenge and review:
For phase-1 deprivation-of-liberty decisions, check the Review Tribunal route and safeguards in the current Code, forms and interim guidance. For another type of decision, obtain advice about the applicable law rather than extending phase-1 powers by analogy.

Sources:
https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/topics/mental-capacity-act
https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/articles/mental-capacity-act-faqs
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nia/2016/18/contents

printableTemplates.title: Restrictions and Liberty
printableTemplates.summary: Describe actual restrictions, identify the setting-specific legal authority, test alternatives and make representation and review practical.
printableTemplates.body:
Restrictions and Liberty
Northern Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The operative deprivation-of-liberty provisions of the Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016 require the relevant assessments, authorisation and safeguards. Setting, age, purpose and the applicable mental-health or children’s framework must be established before selecting a route.

The Department of Health states that the Supreme Court judgment of 2 June 2026 changed the previous approach to defining deprivation of liberty. Interim guidance is available while the Code and other material are reviewed. Read that guidance with current Trust specialist advice; an older training slide is not sufficient evidence of the current legal test.

Local pathway:
Describe actual arrangements and obtain evidence about the person’s wishes, understanding and objections.
Consult the current interim guidance before deciding whether the arrangements amount to deprivation of liberty.
Use the appropriate trained assessors, Trust process and current forms where an authorisation is required.
Keep capacity, best interests, authorisation, consultation and challenge arrangements separately recorded.

Recording prompts:
1. Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
Notes:

2. The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
Notes:

3. Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
Notes:

4. Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
Notes:

5. Representation, review date, expiry and challenge
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Identify the nominated person, advocacy or representation required and the person’s access to the Review Tribunal. Check expiry, review and changed circumstances. Do not remove an existing safeguard solely because a judgment or guidance has changed without the responsible legal review.

Sources:
https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/publications/interim-guidance-mental-capacity-act-ni-2016
https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/articles/mental-capacity-act-faqs

printableTemplates.title: Mental Health
printableTemplates.summary: Distinguish voluntary care, compulsory assessment, detention and treatment; connect the local criteria to evidence and explain the person’s review rights.
printableTemplates.body:
Mental Health
Northern Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Mental Health (Northern Ireland) Order 1986 remains relevant alongside the partly commenced capacity legislation. Assessment and treatment routes have their own criteria and professional roles. For admission for assessment, the Order includes mental disorder of a nature or degree warranting detention for assessment and the relevant substantial likelihood of serious physical harm.

An approved social worker has specific training and functions. The medical recommendation, application and hospital processes should be distinguished. A general referral to mental-health services is not a compulsory admission application.

Local pathway:
Identify voluntary support and whether an assessment or treatment detention route is actually being considered.
Check the current Order, evidence for the particular criteria and the authorised professional’s role.
Keep the partly commenced capacity framework and any separate physical-treatment decision distinct.
Explain the person’s status and arrange rights information, support and review under the applicable route.

Recording prompts:
1. Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
Notes:

2. The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
Notes:

3. Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
Notes:

4. Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
Notes:

5. Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The Review Tribunal and the relevant hospital discharge or review processes address detention questions. Help the person obtain advice and understand how to challenge the measure. Confirm which rules apply to their specific admission status and documents.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nisi/1986/595/contents
https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/mental-health-services-and-support

printableTemplates.title: Adult Safeguarding
printableTemplates.summary: Recognise abuse, neglect and coercion; choose the correct local reporting route; connect immediate protection to the adult’s wishes and continuing support.
printableTemplates.body:
Adult Safeguarding
Northern Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The regional policy Adult Safeguarding: Prevention and Protection in Partnership distinguishes an adult at risk of harm from an adult in need of protection. It considers personal characteristics and life circumstances, with HSC Trust and PSNI roles according to the concern. It is not a general power to compel an adult to accept services.

The Adult Protection Bill is a reform to monitor, not a source of powers to assume are already operational. The Assembly’s legislative tracker must be checked for passage and any subsequent Act and commencement before applying a new duty.

Local pathway:
Identify abuse, exploitation or neglect and the adult’s ability to protect themselves in their actual circumstances.
Use the organisation’s safeguarding arrangements and refer protection concerns to the appropriate HSC Trust route.
Contact PSNI where the circumstances require a police response, distinguishing criminal investigation from the support plan.
Establish the lawful basis for information sharing and for any proposed intervention without agreement.

Recording prompts:
1. Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
Notes:

2. Immediate safety and a safe communication method
Notes:

3. The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
Notes:

4. Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
Notes:

5. Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Use the policy’s participation and proportionate-response approach, together with the applicable consent, capacity and legal safeguards. Explain the Trust or provider complaint process and obtain specialist advice if a coercive intervention is proposed.

Sources:
https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/publications/adult-safeguarding-prevention-and-protection-partnership-key-documents
https://www.niassembly.gov.uk/assembly-business/legislation/2022-2027-mandate/primary-legislation-bills-22-27-mandate/

printableTemplates.title: Children, Families and Transitions
printableTemplates.summary: Separate family support from protection powers, apply the local reporting duty, involve the child and coordinate education, health and transition planning.
printableTemplates.body:
Children, Families and Transitions
Northern Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Children (Northern Ireland) Order 1995 provides the main framework for children in need, family support and protective court processes. Co-operating to Safeguard Children and Young People supplies the regional policy framework. The HSC Trust’s children’s services and PSNI have different responsibilities.

Assessment and family support should be distinguished from a protection investigation or court order. A family meeting cannot create powers of removal or determine legal parental responsibility. Check the child’s position and the relevant authority for accommodation, contact and treatment decisions.

Local pathway:
Record the child’s account, daily experience, harm concerns and support needs.
Use the current regional policy and Trust referral procedure for a child-protection concern.
Identify who holds parental responsibility and any court order affecting the proposed decision.
Coordinate education, health and family support and plan transitions before a service ends.

Recording prompts:
1. Child’s account, communication and daily-life evidence
Notes:

2. Harm, strengths, needs and alternative explanations
Notes:

3. Reporting duty, recipient and action taken
Notes:

4. Family participation, culture and legal authority
Notes:

5. Named plan, education/health links and transition dates
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain the particular assessment, protection or court process, including how the child and family can participate, obtain advocacy or legal advice and raise disagreement. Do not promise confidentiality that conflicts with a necessary safeguarding response.

Sources:
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/nisi/1995/755/contents
https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/publications/co-operating-safeguard-children-and-young-people-northern-ireland

printableTemplates.title: Rights, Culture and Recording
printableTemplates.summary: Connect rights to an actual service decision, distinguish privacy from absolute secrecy and write a record that makes reasons and disagreement visible.
printableTemplates.body:
Rights, Culture and Recording
Northern Ireland practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Northern Ireland has its own equality laws. The Equality Act 2010 does not apply. Identify the relevant disability, sex, race, religious or political discrimination provision and the setting it covers. Section 75 of the Northern Ireland Act 1998 places equality-of-opportunity and good-relations duties on designated public authorities.

The Human Rights Act and applicable UK data-protection law also matter, but they answer different questions. A public authority’s equality scheme does not by itself establish permission to disclose a person’s health information.

Local pathway:
Identify the relevant equality law and public-authority duty for the actual decision.
Arrange accessible communication and consider the applicable reasonable-adjustment obligations.
Establish the purpose and legal basis of sharing, including the treatment of sensitive information.
Record the person’s account, alternatives, reasons, disagreement and the route for correction or challenge.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, affected rights and responsible organisation
Notes:

2. Accessibility, culture and participation arrangements
Notes:

3. Disclosure purpose, legal basis, recipient and limits
Notes:

4. Evidence, alternatives, reasons and disagreement
Notes:

5. Access, correction, complaints and review route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The Equality Commission for Northern Ireland provides information on discrimination and routes to challenge. Distinguish a service complaint, an equality-scheme concern and legal proceedings; obtain timely advice because different limits and remedies apply.

Sources:
https://equalityni.org/equality-laws-ni
https://equalityni.org/public-authorities/section-75
https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/1998/47/section/75
